definition: Force majeure ('greater force' in French) is a standard contract clause that releases both parties from liability when extraordinary, uncontrollable events — such as war or natural disaster — prevent one or both from fulfilling their contractual obligations.
core_idea: A force majeure clause protects contract counterparties from breach liability when performance is made impossible by events outside anyone's control.
key_points: Common in energy and other commercial contracts.
Covers events like wars and natural disasters.
Applies specifically to events outside the control of either contracting party.
relationships: Relevant contract-risk concept alongside weather-driven disruptions discussed in this section.
trading_implications: Traders and structurers should check whether a physical delivery or supply contract includes a force majeure clause, since it determines liability if extreme weather or disaster prevents performance.
